cim_eredeti: Contemporary accomplices? Considering the potential liability of AI targeting system providers under the Rome Statute
szoveg_eredeti:
Artificial intelligence (AI)-enabled targeting systems are increasingly being used in armed conflicts to process data and provide lists of military objectives. This raises a difficult question that has received little attention: Could the senior executives of the technology companies that provide these systems face criminal liability under international law when their systems contribute to serious violations of international humanitarian law?

In this post, part of our Emerging Voices series, Rosa Villar Orero, PhD candidate at the University of Aberdeen, argues that Article 25(3)(d)(ii) of the Rome Statute, as operationalized through the Katanga test, offers a potential doctrinal avenue for establishing the criminal liability of AI targeting system providers whose contribution is made with knowledge of a group’s intention to commit such crimes.

In 1946, a British military tribunal convicted Bruno Tesch for complicity in the murder of millions of people at Auschwitz. Tesch was a businessman who ran Tesch & Stabenow, a company that supplied concentration camps with a poisonous gas called Zyklon B. Although he never entered a camp and never issued an order to kill, merely sat in his office, processed contracts, and shipped chemicals, he was nonetheless found liable. The reasoning was simple: Tesch had knowingly provided the means by which others committed mass atrocity. Physical proximity to the crime was not relevant; what mattered was the structural relationship between his conduct and the crime.

Nearly eighty years later, the question that emerges is: what would Tesch look like today? He would not be selling chemicals. Instead, would he be selling algorithms? As AI services are increasingly used by parties to armed conflict in the conduct of hostilities, it is time to take a fresh look at the precedent for holding companies that provide products and services to warring parties accountable for their contribution, in the case that those parties commit serious violations of international humanitarian law.

In contemporary armed conflicts, AI-enabled targeting systems are being deployed to process vast amounts of data to generate lists of military objectives. These systems dramatically increase the speed and scale of target production. They correlate data, find patterns, and recommend targets – in some reported cases, at a rate that human analysts could never match.

Behind these systems stand technology corporations. Their executives are not in the field or issuing strike orders. They are sitting in urban centers often far from the physical site of attacks, approving contracts. Yet, if these systems are deployed in the commission of war crimes at a large scale, the support those technologies provide becomes legally significant, bringing the following question:

Can the senior executives of technology companies whose AI systems contribute to the commission of war crimes be held criminally liable under the Rome Statute?

The immediate answer that international criminal law offers is Article 25(3)(c) of the Rome Statute: aiding and abetting. But there is a critical problem. Article 25(3)(c) requires that the contributor act for the purpose of facilitating the crime.

Technology corporations are primarily driven by the maximization of profits. Their AI systems are designed and sold as legitimate commercial products. Accordingly, proving that a CEO approved a contract with the purpose of facilitating a war crime is, in practice, evidentially difficult.

The consequence of such a heightened standard is a dangerous gap. Corporations that provide the infrastructure of modern atrocity may escape liability simply by arguing that their business was driven by commercial indifference rather than criminal purpose. This problem, however, is not new. Academia has long grappled with these neutral contributions trying to find an answer for the main question: when do neutral contributions become complicity?

Considering this bottleneck, this post identifies a different provision as the operative avenue. Article 25(3)(d)(ii) provides that a person is criminally responsible if: “In any other way contributes to the commission or attempted commission of such a crime by a group of persons acting with a common purpose. Such contribution shall be intentional and shall either: (i) Be made with the aim of furthering the criminal activity or criminal purpose of the group, where such activity or purpose involves the commission of a crime within the jurisdiction of the Court; or (ii) Be made in the knowledge of the intention of the group to commit the crime.” This is a residual mode of accessorial liability that has received comparatively little scholarly attention.

Unlike subparagraph (c), this provision does not require purpose. It requires knowledge – specifically, that the contribution was made with knowledge of the group’s intention to commit the crime.

This is not a radical departure. It is, in fact, the return to the standard applied by the tribunals that convicted Tesch. Moreover, this provision was operationalized by Trial Chamber II in Katanga. Katanga arose from the ICC’s prosecution of Germain Katanga, a Congolese militia commander, for war crimes and a crime against humanity committed during the 2003 attack on Bogoro, a village in the Ituri district of the Democratic Republic of Congo. In its 2014 judgment, Trial Chamber II shifted his mode of liability from principal perpetration to accessorial liability under Article 25(3)(d). This was the first instance in which the provision was substantively interpreted and in doing so, the Chamber developed a five-element test.

This post argues that this test, properly understood and extended, reaches the conduct of senior executives of technology corporations. However, before applying it, doctrinal foundations need to be established.

AI systems are provided by corporations, but the Rome Statute only holds natural persons liable under Article 25(1). Corporate criminal liability was deliberately excluded from the Statute.

However, the exclusion was not a denial of the role played by companies; it was a design choice that requires identifying the right individual within the corporation. The natural person who held effective decision-making power – the executive who authorized or had the power to veto the provision of the system. The I.G. Farben standard, developed after the Second World War, provides the template: a defendant is liable if they were a participant in the act, or, being aware of it, had the authority to prevent it and failed to do so.

The Zyklon B tribunal inferred Tesch’s knowledge from his professional position and the public context of the atrocities being committed. However, the Krupp case refined this and established that it cannot be inferred from the defendant’s official position alone, but it must be proved that the contributor “knowingly participated”.

Accordingly, the knowledge-based mens rea proposed in this post does not emerge in a vacuum; it was developed through the jurisprudence of post-WWII military tribunals, later consolidated by the ad hoc tribunals, and now forms part of customary international law.

With those foundations in place, the five elements of the Katanga test can be applied to AI-enabled targeting systems, and grounded in contemporary conflicts.

Element (i): A crime within the jurisdiction of the Court was committed. The ICC has issued arrest warrants in contemporary armed conflicts for the war crime of intentionally attacking civilians under Article 8(2)(b).

Element (ii): The persons who committed the crime belonged to a group acting with a common purpose. Trial Chamber II in Katanga argued that the existence of such group “would be evidenced without necessarily establishing the existence of an organization incorporated into a military, political or administrative structure”. cim: Büntetőjogi felelősségre vonhatók a katonai AI-t biztosító cégvezetők
lead: Egy új jogi elemzés szerint a Római Statútum alapján a háborús bűnökért az AI-alapú célkiválasztó rendszereket szállító cégek vezetői is felelősségre vonhatók.
osszefoglalo:
A fegyveres konfliktusokban egyre gyakrabban használnak mesterséges intelligenciával működő célkiválasztó rendszereket, amelyek drasztikusan felgyorsítják a katonai célpontok azonosítását. Egy [friss jogi elemzés](https://blogs.icrc.org/law-and-policy/2026/10/29/contemporary-accomplices-considering-the-potential-liability-of-ai-targeting-system-providers-under-the-rome-statute/) azt vizsgálja, hogy a technológiai vállalatok felsővezetői büntetőjogilag felelősségre vonhatók-e a Nemzetközi Büntetőbíróság előtt, ha rendszereik hozzájárulnak a nemzetközi humanitárius jog súlyos megsértéséhez.

A tanulmány rámutat, hogy bár a cégvezetők nem közvetlenül a harctéren hozzák meg a döntéseket, a **Római Statútum 25. cikk (3)(d)(ii) bekezdése** alapján bűnsegédként elítélhetők. Ehhez nem szükséges bizonyítani, hogy a vezető szándékosan a bűncselekmény elősegítéséért kötött szerződést, elegendő az a tény, ha tudomása volt a rendszert használó csoport bűnös szándékáról.

Ez a jogi megközelítés a második világháború utáni Zyklon B-per előzményeire nyúlik vissza, ahol a vegyi anyagot szállító cégvezetőt pusztán a tudatos adásvétel miatt ítélték el. Mivel a **nemzetközi jog** egyéni büntetőjogi felelősséget állapít meg, a döntéshozó cégvezetők személyesen is felelősségre vonhatók.
miert_szamit: Ez a jogi értelmezés **alapjaiban változtathatja meg a védelmi célú AI-fejlesztések kockázatait**, és szigorúbb ellenőrzésre kényszerítheti a katonai szoftvereket értékesítő technológiai cégeket.

prioritas.indok: Nemzetközi jogi és etikai kérdést vizsgál az mesterséges intelligenciát gyártó cégek felelősségéről fegyveres konfliktusokban. Forrás-tapasztalat: -7.
prioritas.cim_hu: Büntethetővé válhatnak-e a katonai AI-t fejlesztő cégvezetők a nemzetközi jog szerint
prioritas.lead_hu: Egy új elemzés azt vizsgálja, hogy a katonai célpontválasztó AI-rendszereket beszállító technológiai vállalatok vezetői büntetőjogi felelősségre vonhatók-e a Római Statútum alapján.

tenyellenorzes.esemeny: Rosa Villar Orero jogi elemzésben vizsgálta meg, hogy a Római Statútum alapján büntetőjogilag felelősségre vonhatók-e a katonai AI-célkiválasztó rendszereket szállító cégek felsővezetői, ha rendszereik hozzájárulnak a nemzetközi humanitárius jog súlyos megsértéséhez.
